decision.reason: For the direct replication of Liberman and Trope (1998, Study 1) on the 19-item BIF (omitting the original free-writing task and administering the 6 excluded BIF items on a separate page), the authors evaluated the replication against two explicit preregistered criteria—consistency in direction and consistency in magnitude—within an overall 'limited support' synthesis. They explicitly conclude that the temporal-distance replication effect was consistent in direction (d = 0.08, 95% CI [0.003, 0.16]; d = 0.12, 95% CI [0.06, 0.19] after valence adjustment) but inconsistent in magnitude with the original effect (d = 0.92, only 9% of the original size, with the replication CI upper bound excluding 0.92). Moreover, excluding the 21.5% comprehension-check failures caused the 95% CI to include zero (d = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.004, 0.17]), and item-level analyses showed 5 of 19 BIF items with CIs excluding zero in the predicted direction versus 5 of 19 in the opposite direction. Under the codebook, because the authors themselves present the Liberman & Trope (1998, Study 1) evidence as partly supporting (direction) and partly not supporting (magnitude and robustness) rather than as an unqualified success or the social-distance failure quoted in the shipped row, the outcome is 'mixed'.

decision.reason: Because the study is a reproduction, its outcome is evaluated on the two reproduction axes while accounting for the reconstructed sample differences. On outcome_computation, re-running Kolk's (2019) visualizations and OLS/country-fixed-effects specifications in R on the reconstructed 35-country HFD and V-Dem v7.1 panel (2,054 vs. 1,993 cumulative country-years due to 61 newer TFR observations and unspecified original country periods, plus minor pre-1960 differences in Spain and Portugal) closely recovers Kolk's results—confirming a negative within-country relationship and weak support for a U-shape with WPEI, which the author characterizes as demonstrating 'a high level of verifiability and low inaccuracy' ('computationally reproducible'). On outcome_robustness, substituting the multidimensional HGEI (32 countries, 1,280 country-years, 1950-2003) and tempo-adjusted TFR (24 countries, 649 country-years) and adding country fixed effects and country-specific time trends (Models 1.4 and 2.4) overturns Kolk's (2019) substantive conclusion by revealing a statistically significant conditional within-country U-shaped relationship ('robustness challenges').

decision.reason: The paper separates its independent replication in 2,470 Spanish individuals from a pooled 12-study meta-analysis (N = 31,771) that incorporates Lambert et al.'s (2009) original cohorts and public GWAS datasets. Under the codebook, pooled meta-analysis support including original data cannot be transferred as an unqualified verdict on the independent new-sample retest. In the Spanish replication sample alone, the authors explicitly state that 'Overall, the CR1 rs3818361 marker was not significantly associated to AD in this sample of the Spanish population' (P > .16 across all unadjusted comparisons and P > .60 across all age-, sex-, and APOE-adjusted logistic regression models), with point estimates in the opposite direction when comparing cases against neuropsychologically healthy elderly controls (OR = 0.877, P = .43 allelic; OR = 0.856, P = .43 dominant) and in all adjusted models (OR = 0.894-0.990). At the same time, they report a nonsignificant crude allelic trend comparing cases to general-population controls (OR = 1.114, 95% CI 0.958-1.296, P = .16) whose direction and modest magnitude they describe as concordant with Lambert et al. [1] under a winner's-curse interpretation. Because the independent Spanish retest is overall statistically null with opposing point estimates in NHEC/adjusted comparisons alongside a concordant crude allelic trend, the independent replication outcome is 'mixed'.

In this study, we have first implemented a Google Colab Pro compatible version of the authors’ code, enabling us to
train and test StyleGAN2 and the two flavours of GANformer (Duplex and Simplex attention) in less than 54 hours in
total. As presented in Section 5, we could not achieve the improvements declared by the authors but instead found a
decrease in time performance and quality using duplex attention.
Believing it was an error arising from our adaptation, we have analysed the pre-trained models provided and noticed
what we think are discrepancies between the code and the methodology discussed in the paper.
In “Generative Adversarial Transformers” by Hudson and Zitnick [2], the attention component is said to be placed both
on the Generator and the discriminator sub-networks. At the same time, in all the pre-trained models provided, it seems
never to be used on the discriminator.
decision.reason: Note first that the paper reproduces Hudson and Zitnick (2021, Generative Adversarial Transformers, arXiv:2103.01209, Ref. [2]); the shipped doi_o (10.1016/b978-0-12-823519-5.00003-8, Aarti 2021) is an unreferenced bibliographic mislink on this row, while type 'reproduction' is established from the reuse of Hudson and Zitnick's code, pre-trained models, and FFHQ dataset. Crucially, due to single-GPU Google Colab Pro limits, the authors did not run an identical original computation: they merged and simplified the codebase, discarded three of the four original datasets and four baselines, downsampled FFHQ from 256x256 to 128x128 (and added a non-original 64x64 Cartoon dataset), and trained for 300 kimg rather than up to 10,000 kimg over multiple V100 GPU-days. Thus, inferior performance under reduced resolution/training does not by itself prove failure of the identical full-scale computation. Instead, outcome_computation: 'computational issues' rests on the direct discrepancies identified between the published paper and the authors' released code and pre-trained models: the codebase specifies different Adam hyperparameters (beta_1=0.0, beta_2=0.99, epsilon=10^-8) than reported in the paper (beta_1=0.9, beta_2=0.999, epsilon=10^-3; Table 1), and none of the released pre-trained models use attention in the discriminator despite the paper stating attention is applied in both generator and discriminator (plus Cityscapes 256x256 training exceeded 25 GB GPU memory). On outcome_robustness, under the adapted 128x128, 300-kimg training regime on FFHQ (Table 5)—including the architectural variant removing discriminator attention to match the pre-trained weights—Duplex GANformer yielded worse FID (53.48 and 43.66 vs. 40.22) and slower training per step than baseline StyleGAN2 ('robustness challenges').
